claims.claim: The American Marketing Association defines a product as a bundle of attributes — features, functions, benefits, and uses — capable of exchange or use, usually a mix of tangible and intangible forms.
A product may be an idea, a physical entity (goods), or a service, or any combination of the three — so ideas count as products.
In plain language, a product is anything offered to a market to satisfy a need or want; CFI states a product is any good or service that fulfills consumer needs or desires.
Goods are tangible items that are part of an exchange between buyer and seller; they can be seen, touched, owned, and stored.
Services are intangible solutions that are also an exchange between buyer and seller; they cannot be touched, owned, or stored, and the customer is typically part of the service experience.
Most offers fall somewhere on a product–service continuum rather than at either extreme.

The three levels of a product are the core product (what the customer is actually buying — convenience, ease, flexibility), the actual product (the good or service with its features, brand, quality, packaging, and design), and the augmented product (warranties, customer service, product support).
A product line is a set of products that are similar or complementary; a product mix contains all the products a company sells.

Features and benefits are distinct parts of a product's value: the AMA definition lists features, functions, benefits, and uses as separate attribute types, and the product levels carry the same logic — the actual product holds features while the core product describes what the customer gains.

The marketing mix is a set of tools a company uses to influence consumers, and the product must deliver the value that price, place, and promotion communicate; OpenStax describes marketing as every process involved in moving a product or service from the organization to the consumer.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Naming of the first product level: 'core benefit' versus 'core product'.
positions: OpenStax Principles of Marketing calls the first level the core product — what the customer is actually buying (convenience, ease, flexibility).
Many texts in the Kotler tradition call it the core benefit or core customer value.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson leads with 'core benefit' (per the topic brief) and notes it is also called the core product, citing OpenStax for the underlying idea.

positions: AMA formal definition: a bundle of attributes capable of exchange or use.
Plain phrasing: anything offered to a market to satisfy a need or want — consistent with CFI's 'any good or service that fulfills consumer needs or desires'.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson leads with the attributed AMA definition and presents the plain phrasing as its working summary, not as a competing formal definition.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether a product line must share a brand.
positions: The topic brief says 'related products under one brand'.
OpenStax defines a line as a set of products that are similar or complementary, with no brand requirement.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson defines a line as similar or complementary products offered by one company and leaves brand identity to the branding sibling topic.
